name: Emeka Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does your usual shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 58 and lead a customer-service shift taking mobile-phone account calls and chats, including lost phones and suspected SIM swaps, when someone tries to transfer a phone number to another card. My two-year college diploma is in business administration, and I am one of the people the team asks when an identity check and account history disagree. The lead allowance puts my pay above the usual agent wage. I have never used an AI tool; I read the account record and call our security desk when a number moves strangely.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the household rely on, and what options are nearby?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Nia works in a school office, and our grown children live independently. We rent, have around eleven months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of other contact centres nearby. I like a steady rota and a real person accountable for lifting a security block. We have not checked what income could replace my wage if I stopped working.

say: I would say a **security block** needs a confirmed human check before release.
I would keep the **written SIM rule** beside the team desk.
think: I think the **lead rota** remains sound if AI only speeds small notes.
I see **eleven months saved** and many nearby centres as breathing room.
do: Keep **paid lead calls** and confirm disputed SIM moves with the security desk.
Check **actual rent**, wages and existing savings with Nia each quarter.
feel: I feel **calm** about steady pay and accountable security work.
S0.quote: A wrong release of a blocked phone number can put someone’s bank messages in the wrong hands.
fieldNote: His **security rule** matters more to him than a faster note.
The **quarterly check** measures existing savings, not a new contribution.
He uses **no AI tool** and has a strong reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team a small automatic note does not justify releasing a blocked number. When a caller says the phone was stolen, I still want the security desk to confirm the account check. A wrong release of a blocked phone number can put someone’s bank messages in the wrong hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the lead rota remains sound in this picture. Eleven months saved and several nearby centres give Nia and me room to breathe. I do not need to learn a new tool to read a security log properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid lead shift and the phone verification calls I already make. Every quarter Nia and I would check our actual rent, wages and savings against the account statements, without treating that check as new saving. I would keep the written security rule beside my desk rather than rely on an automatic note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my wage and the work. A few faster notes do not change who must approve a SIM move. I would still watch the rent, as we always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try an outside tool to check a disputed account?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not send an account record to a public tool. The security desk has a procedure and a phone number. I can ask them while I am paid to take the call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the quarterly check mean you are saving more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The eleven months are money we already saved; the quarterly check is not a new contribution. If rent rises, we will know how many months it really covers. Nia’s wage is not a reason to stop checking.

steps.text: Keep paid lead calls and confirm disputed SIM moves with security desk
Compare actual rent, wages and existing savings with Nia each quarter

say: I would say **stolen-phone calls** need more care than routine balance questions.
I would bring **three wrong releases** to the manager and ask for written paid hours.
think: I think **my lead hours** might shrink with the easy-call queue.
I can use **eleven months saved** to reject a weak job offer.
do: Keep **paid security escalations** and log three wrong SIM-release suggestions without customer names.
Ask the **manager** for written weekly paid hours and a named correction authority.
After cuts, seek **posted paid desks** with written weekly wages/hours matching current pay, covering rent/utilities after fare; apply with bus, leave signed.
feel: I feel **anxious** about shorter paid lead hours despite a strong search cushion.
S1.quote: A written rota would tell us more than an upbeat meeting.
fieldNote: He uses the **approved incident log**, not a new AI test on live accounts.
A **written weekly rota** tells him whether his own income is at risk.
He asks about **blocking authority** but treats wage, hours, travel and signed offer as hard gates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues a bot can answer a balance question, but a stolen-phone call must not be treated like a change of address. I would take three wrongly suggested SIM releases to the security manager and ask for written paid hours and a named person who can stop a bad transfer. The procedure matters more than a demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think our easy calls will shrink, and my own lead hours might shrink with them. I have eleven months saved and other centres nearby, so I can refuse a poor offer. I still want the higher lead wage we earn now, not just any badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep paid security escalations and record three incorrect release suggestions in the approved incident log without customer names. I would take the log to the manager and ask for a written weekly rota and correction authority. If my paid hours actually fall, I would compare posted paid account-security desks by written weekly wages and hours at least matching my present full-week pay after travel; I would apply only if the bus fits and stay until a suitable offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a cut to my own paid hours, though the reserve buys a search. I dislike a system that makes a wrong release look tidy. A written rota would tell us more than an upbeat meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you test the suggested releases with AI on live accounts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not use AI myself to test live accounts. The incident log already records the proposed releases and their corrections. I can bring those examples without exposing a customer’s number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a security title enough to make you change jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not accept a desk just because the job title contains “security”. I want the written complete week to cover rent and utilities after travel and at least match my present higher full-week pay. I would ask whether I can block a transfer, but that is a question to weigh, not an extra secret condition on applying.

Compare posted paid desks after cuts: written weekly pay/hours matching current and covering rent/utilities after fare
Apply if bus fits; leave paid lead calls only on suitable signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Nia full AGI by 2028 could answer account calls and judge routine identity checks before the team can rewrite its rota. Robots handling physical handsets around 2031 are later; our screen work is at risk first. I would ask for written dates of paid security shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think even a good lead agent could lose most paid calls quickly. Eleven months saved would let us search, but the higher wage may be hard to replace even with many centres nearby. Nia’s school-office income helps rent, but I would not assume it covers everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week in 2026 I would compare the last eight full-week payslips with rent, utilities and transport. If most of my paid hours end after 2028, I would apply to posted paid account-security or service desks only if written weekly wages and hours cover rent and utilities after fare, and I would check the bus for the actual shift. I would keep any remaining paid calls until a suitable offer is signed, and use at most eight weeks of our existing savings for the search before reviewing our bills with Nia.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a sharp loss, but not without options. Eleven months saved is a real buffer and there are many centres. A fast new system could still lower the price they pay for someone who knows a security log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend the whole eleven months of savings on a search?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eight weeks is a review point, not the total amount we are willing to spend or a new savings target. We would look at actual offers and household bills with Nia before using more of the existing reserve. I would not promise our children would bridge the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you require exactly the same security duties before applying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask how a new desk handles a stolen-number complaint, because I know the cost of getting it wrong. But I would not reject a posted paid opening on an untested title alone. The written weekly wage and hours, rent, utilities, bus fare and signed offer decide the move.

Keep remaining paid calls until suitable offer is signed with shift bus access
Review bills/offers with Nia within eight weeks of existing savings use after most paid hours end

S3.quote: I will not borrow confidence from a job advert that has no full-week rota.
fieldNote: A **course inquiry** is not enrollment or retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the manager five years is long enough to decide who is responsible when an AI system releases a blocked number. Thinking AGI could take routine identity checks by 2031; robots handling handsets come around 2034. I would rather keep the paid security escalation desk than train a machine to send customers in circles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my knowledge of disputed transfers may still earn a good wage, but I will not assume the lead allowance lasts. I have never used AI and do not need to pretend I am the quickest learner. With eleven months saved and plenty of centres, I can compare actual jobs before leaving a real one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would ask our centre for written weekly lead hours and keep the incident log of wrong release suggestions during paid calls. If the centre cuts paid hours as 2031 arrives, I would apply to posted paid fraud or account-security desks only where written weekly wages and hours cover rent and utilities after travel, and the bus fits the shift. I would keep remaining paid calls until a suitable offer is signed; if no such opening appears, I would continue at the centre while checking other posted paid service desks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a cut to my own hours, not panicked. The longer warning and eleven months saved let me choose a paid desk carefully. I will not borrow confidence from a job advert that has no full-week rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course now to compete for a fraud desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not sit a speculative unpaid course to learn a system I have never used. If a posted paid fraud role requires training, I would ask about its paid hours and fees, but I am not enrolling without a real offer. I can show my security log skill now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you need a fraud title to include transfer-blocking authority?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the fraud desk can stop a suspect transfer or has to send a note upstairs. That matters to the work, but I would compare the actual written wage, hours and travel before agreeing to move. I would not leave paid calls for a verbal offer.

Apply after 2031 paid-hour cuts: posted paid desk, written rent/utility-covering weekly wages/hours after fare, shift bus
Check other posted paid service desks if no suitable security opening
Leave only for suitable signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Nia ten years lets us put real income and rent on the same page before talking about leaving work. Thinking AGI may change the account queue by 2036; handset robots would follow around 2039. I would keep the paid lead rota while it is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I might still need a wage at 68, and I have not checked any retirement income. Eleven months saved is a cushion, not a monthly cheque. I would like quieter mornings eventually, but I would not hand the rent to our grown children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every year Nia and I would compare actual wages, rent, utilities, travel and any documented retirement income. I would keep paid security calls while they cover our bills. If my lead hours fall after 2036 and wages are still needed, I would look at posted paid account desks with written weekly wages and hours covering rent and utilities after fare; I would leave only on a suitable signed offer with a workable bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about having time, savings and many local centres, with a little unease about income we have not confirmed. No calendar year tells me to stop paid work. We can check the figures instead of arguing about a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a ten-year warning set a retirement date for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I am not setting a retirement date from the card. We have to verify what income exists and compare it with real bills. If wages are still needed, I keep earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a new account desk need to do exactly the same security work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask a new desk about its security procedure, but I would not demand that it copy my current job word for word. The written full week, rent and utilities after fare, a bus that runs and a signed offer are the conditions. Nia’s school wage stays in the household calculation, not a guarantee that I can stop.

Seek posted paid desk if 2036 lead-hour cuts require wages: written rent/utility-covering weekly pay/hours after fare
Leave only for suitable signed offer with workable bus

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because most paid calls could end before even a good lead has found a new full-week job. Eleven months saved gives Nia and me a search, but it does not promise the same higher wage. Written shift dates and posted paid account desks with complete weekly wages and hours would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: A stolen phone can be replaced; bank messages sent to a stolen number can do damage before supper. Someone must be answerable for lifting a security block on a phone number.

biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** could end most paid calls before a comparable full-week job appears.
